learn: A force is a push or a pull. Forces can start motion, stop it, or change its direction.
Kicking a ball is a push. Opening a drawer is a pull.
Forces have a strength (size) and a direction.
check: Forces have a strength and a...
lessons.try: List five pushes and five pulls you make in a day.

learn: Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward Earth's centre.
When you drop a ball, gravity pulls it down.
Gravity keeps us on the ground and keeps the Moon orbiting Earth.
check: What keeps us on the ground?
lessons.try: Drop a ball and a crumpled piece of paper from the same height. Watch them fall.

learn: Friction is a force that slows down objects rubbing against each other.
Rough surfaces like carpet make more friction than smooth surfaces like ice.
Friction lets shoes grip the ground and brakes stop a bike.
check: What uses friction to stop a bike?
lessons.try: Slide a toy car on carpet and on a smooth floor. Where does it go farther?

learn: When forces on an object are equal and opposite, they are balanced.
Balanced forces don't change motion. A book on a table stays still because gravity pulls down and the table pushes up equally.
In a tug of war where both teams pull equally, the rope doesn't move.
check: Why does a book on a table stay still?
In an even tug of war, the rope...
lessons.try: Play a gentle tug of war with even teams. What happens?

learn: When one force is stronger, the forces are unbalanced.
Unbalanced forces change motion: an object starts, stops, speeds up, slows down or turns.
Kicking a still ball creates an unbalanced force that makes it move.
check: A harder push makes a toy car go...
Which is an example of unbalanced forces?
A book resting on a table
lessons.try: Push a toy car gently and then harder. Compare how far it goes.

learn: Forces can be measured with a spring scale, in units called newtons.
A bigger force stretches the spring more.
Scientists measure forces to compare and predict motion.
check: A bigger force stretches the spring...
lessons.try: Make a rubber band scale and compare how far it stretches pulling different objects.

learn: Motion is a change in position.
We describe position with words like above, below, left and right, or with distance from a point.
Speed is how fast an object changes position.
lessons.try: Roll a ball and measure how far it goes in 3 seconds.

learn: Some motions repeat in patterns.
A swing goes back and forth. A pendulum swings in a regular rhythm.
Because the pattern repeats, we can predict where it will be next.
check: Why can we predict a pendulum?
lessons.try: Make a pendulum with string and a washer. Count swings in 15 seconds.

learn: Scientists observe patterns to predict future motion.
A ball rolling down a ramp always speeds up. A higher ramp makes it faster.
Recording data in a table helps find patterns.
check: A higher ramp makes a ball go...
lessons.try: Roll a ball down ramps of different heights. Record the distance it rolls.

learn: Magnets attract objects made of iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Opposite poles attract. Like poles repel.
Magnetic force can act without touching, even through paper.
check: Can magnetic force act through paper?
lessons.try: Test ten objects to see which a magnet attracts.

learn: Magnets are used in fridge doors, compasses, speakers and motors.
A compass needle is a magnet that points north because Earth is like a giant magnet.
Engineers use magnets to solve problems, like a latch that keeps a cupboard closed.
check: Why does a compass point north?
Earth acts like a giant magnet
lessons.try: Design a magnetic latch for a box.

learn: Static electricity is a build-up of electric charge on an object.
Rubbing a balloon on your hair gives it charge, and it can stick to a wall or lift tiny paper bits.
Like charges repel and opposite charges attract, just like magnet poles.
check: Rubbing a balloon on hair creates...
lessons.try: Rub a balloon on your hair and try to pick up small paper pieces.

learn: A life cycle is the stages a living thing goes through: birth, growth, reproduction and death.
A plant starts as a seed, germinates into a seedling, grows into an adult plant, makes flowers and seeds, and the cycle repeats.
Germination is when a seed begins to sprout.
check: When a seed begins to sprout
A life cycle includes birth, growth, reproduction and...
lessons.try: Grow a bean in a clear cup with a wet paper towel and draw each stage.

learn: Some insects go through complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult.
A butterfly's larva is a caterpillar. Its pupa is a chrysalis.
Beetles, bees and butterflies all have complete metamorphosis.
lessons.try: Draw the four stages of a butterfly's life cycle.

learn: A frog goes from egg to tadpole to froglet to adult frog.
Grasshoppers have incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult. Nymphs look like small adults.
Mammals are born alive and grow into adults. Their babies look like small adults.
check: A grasshopper's middle stage is a...
lessons.try: Compare the life cycle of a frog and a human.

learn: Traits are features of living things.
Inherited traits are passed from parents to offspring, like eye colour, fur pattern or leaf shape.
Offspring look similar to parents but have variations.
check: Do offspring look exactly like parents?
lessons.try: Look at family photos. What traits do family members share?

learn: Some traits are learned, like riding a bike or speaking a language.
The environment can change traits: a plant in shade may grow taller and thinner; a well-fed dog grows bigger.
Flamingos are pink because of the food they eat.
lessons.try: Grow two plants, one in sun and one in shade. Compare after two weeks.

learn: Differences among individuals of a species are called variations.
Some variations help survival: a moth with colours matching tree bark is harder for birds to spot.
Those that survive have more offspring, passing on helpful traits.
check: A moth matching tree bark is...
lessons.try: Hide coloured paper "moths" on newspaper. Which are hardest to find?

learn: Fossils are the remains or traces of living things from long ago, preserved in rock.
Bones, shells, leaves, footprints and even dung can become fossils.
Most fossils form in layers of mud or sand that harden into rock.
check: Remains or traces of ancient life
lessons.try: Press a shell into clay to make a model fossil imprint.

learn: Fossils show what plants and animals lived long ago.
Fish fossils on a mountain show the area was once underwater.
Fern fossils in Antarctica show it was once warmer.
check: Fish fossils on a mountain show...
Fern fossils in Antarctica show it was once...
lessons.try: Look at pictures of fossils and guess the environment they lived in.

learn: Extinct means a type of living thing no longer exists anywhere.
Dinosaurs became extinct about 66 million years ago.
Some animals, like the dodo, went extinct more recently. People work to protect endangered animals today.
check: About when did dinosaurs become extinct?
lessons.try: Research one extinct animal and one endangered animal.

learn: An adaptation is a trait that helps a living thing survive in its environment.
Physical adaptations are body parts, like a duck's webbed feet or a cactus's spines.
Behavioural adaptations are actions, like birds migrating or bears hibernating.
lessons.try: Choose an animal and list one physical and one behavioural adaptation.

learn: Many animals live in groups to survive.
Wolves hunt in packs. Fish swim in schools to confuse predators. Bees work together in a hive.
Groups help with finding food, protection and raising young.
check: Why do fish swim in schools?
lessons.try: Act out how a school of fish protects itself.

learn: Environments can change through drought, floods, fires or human building.
When environments change, some organisms survive, some move away and some die.
People can help by protecting habitats and creating wildlife corridors.
lessons.try: Think of a way to help animals near your home, like planting native flowers.

learn: Weather is the condition of the air at a certain time and place: temperature, wind, clouds and precipitation.
Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Meteorologists measure weather with thermometers, rain gauges and wind vanes.
lessons.try: Record the weather every day for a week in a table.

learn: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years.
Deserts have a dry climate. Rainforests have a hot, wet climate. Polar regions have a cold climate.
Weather changes day to day. Climate describes long-term patterns.
check: The usual weather over many years
lessons.try: Compare the climate of your town with a town in another part of the world.

learn: Scientists record data in tables and graphs to find patterns.
A bar graph can show rainfall each month. A line graph can show temperatures.
Patterns help predict what weather a season will bring.
check: What shows temperature changes over time?
lessons.try: Make a bar graph of rainy days over two weeks.

learn: Natural hazards are events in nature that can cause harm.
Hurricanes bring strong winds and heavy rain. Tornadoes are spinning columns of air. Floods happen when water overflows onto land.
Forecasts and warnings give people time to prepare.
check: A spinning column of air is a...
What gives people time to prepare?
lessons.try: Find out which natural hazards are common where you live.

learn: Earthquakes are sudden shaking of the ground.
Volcanoes can erupt with lava, ash and gas.
Landslides happen when soil and rock slide down a slope.
check: What do you do in an earthquake?
Stand in a doorway on a high floor
Soil and rock slide down a slope
lessons.try: Learn "Drop, Cover and Hold On" for earthquakes.

learn: Engineers design solutions to reduce the harm of hazards.
Levees and flood walls hold back water. Lightning rods protect buildings. Strong frames help buildings survive earthquakes.
Families can prepare an emergency kit with water, food, a flashlight and a first-aid kit.
lessons.try: Make a checklist for a family emergency kit.
